To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the sidebands in the photoelectron spectra of laser-assited ionization of atoms cannot be resolved for a short coherence time of the free electron laser ( FEL) pulses, whereas the sidebands in Auger electron spectra are practically independent of FEL pulse coherence.
the temporal coherence influences the line widths of the sidebands in the photoelectron spectra of laser-assist photoionization and Auger decay.
the sidebands in the electron spectrum of the laser-assisted photo- and Augre decay of atoms are influenced by the partial temporal coherence (PTC) of the ionizing radiation.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
for the case of photoionization the coherence of the laser pulse is of crucial importance, while in the case of photoinduced Augeer decay it is of no significance.

the partial temporal coherence is important in the photoelectron and Auger spectra of atoms irradiated by short intense FEL pulses, but the influence of this coherence on the Auger spectra can be ignored.
the partial temporal coherence does not influence the Auger spectra, but does influence the photoelectron spectra.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the temporal coherence influences the photoelectron spectrum but does not change the Auger electron spectra.
the temporal coherence influences the photoelectron spectrum only if it has a sufficiently long coherence time.
the coherence time of a FEL pulse does not influence the photoinduced Augeer decay of atoms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
for the analysis of photoelectron spectra it is essential to take into account the partial temporal coherence, whereas the coherence effects can be neglected for the Auger electron spectra.
the temporal coherence time of a femtosecond FEL pulse can be used as a parameter for controlling the sidebands in the electron spectra.
the coherence properties of FEL pulses can be used for the investigation of the temporal evolution of photoionization and the following Auge decay.
